title: All gone now
hookLine: a king's golden palaces and elephants, every one of them gone
carry: it was grand once, and it's gone

cards: Kusinara was not much of a place. In the Mahaparinibbana Sutta, Ananda pleads with the Buddha: please don't pass away in this little wattle-and-daub town, out in the jungle.
There are great cities: Rajagaha, Savatthi, Varanasi. Go there. And the Buddha says: don't call it that, Ananda.
Long ago, this was a royal city, and he begins to describe it. The seventeenth Long Discourse tells the whole story.

teach.b: The city was called Kusavati, and its king was Mahasudassana, the great and beautiful. The sutta lingers on every detail. Seven walls, of gold, silver, beryl, crystal and more.
Rows of palm trees made of jewels, and when the wind moved their leaves, the sound was sweet and lovely, like a well-played orchestra, so that the people who heard it danced.
Eighty-four thousand cities, eighty-four thousand palaces, eighty-four thousand elephants with golden trappings, chariots, horses, gems, and a whole court around him. The king was good, too.

He gave freely, and in a palace built for him he sat alone and practiced, letting a mind of loving-kindness, compassion, gladness and calm fill every direction: the same practice as the trumpeter on day five hundred forty-two.

teach.h: HE LIVED IN ONLY ONE PALACE.
teach.b: Out of all those palaces, the king lived in only one. Out of all those elephants, he rode only one.
And at the end, the Buddha tells Ananda: I was that king. And see, Ananda, all those things are past, ceased, changed. That is how impermanent conditioned things are.
It's a strange kind of comfort. The Buddha is lying in a poor village, and he doesn't argue that it's secretly grand.
He says it was grand once, and it's gone, as everything grand goes.

Look back at this week: no closed fist, the four great references, the four places, Ananda in the doorway, the teaching as teacher, the relics shared, and now a golden city gone back to mud and thatch.

how: Buddhist teachers often use the Mahasudassana story to teach impermanence, and at funerals in Theravada countries monks chant the verse beginning 'anicca vata sankhara', impermanent indeed are conditioned things.

o: impermanent, bound to pass and change
the sorrow of losing what you loved
a golden city lost beneath the ground

games.q: all gone now: tap the pairs.
p: the jeweled city that was Kusinara
made music when the wind blew

s: the Buddha agrees Kusinara is too humble a place to die
he tells Ananda not to call it that: it was once a royal city.
of all his palaces, the king lived in only one
and rode only one of his many elephants.
King Mahasudassana practiced loving-kindness in every direction
the same four immeasurables as the trumpeter passage.

games.q: Ananda begs you not to die in a humble jungle village. what do you, the Buddha, say?
o: agree, and set off for a great city.
tell him it was once a royal city, and that all its splendor has passed.
say that places don't matter at all.
games.why: he tells the story of Kusavati and ends: all those things are past, ceased, changed.

practice: Look at one fine thing near you, a cup you like, a plant, the light on a wall, kindly and fully, as if it's the best palace in the city.
Then close your eyes and let yourself know it won't last forever, not with sadness, just with honesty. Keep the kindness and the honesty together, and breathe.

wordCard.voice: Anicca. The Mahasudassana Sutta's ending: a king's jeweled city, palaces and elephants, all past, ceased and changed. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali anicca: impermanent. the lesson the Buddha draws from the vanished city.

carryVoice: Your line: it was grand once, and it's gone. A fine thing is no less fine for passing. That closes the week.

sources.ref: Digha Nikaya 16 (Mahaparinibbana Sutta), Ananda's plea about Kusinara
